content: Have you ever wondered how trees grow so big? We eat food to grow, but a tree can't walk to a grocery store or eat a pizza. So, where does its food come from?
If you were a plant stuck in one place, what ingredients around you could you possibly use to make food? Take a guess before moving on!

content.title: The Plant's Secret Kitchen
content.description: An animation showing sunlight hitting a leaf, water travelling up from the roots, and carbon dioxide entering tiny pores (stomata). Inside the leaf, they mix together like ingredients in a kitchen.

content: Plants are like magical chefs. They make their own food using sunlight, water, and air. This process is called Photosynthesis! Because they make their own food, they are called Autotrophs (Auto = self, Trophos = nourishment).

question: Which of the following is NOT an ingredient used by plants to make food?

content: Imagine you are a leaf for a day. Explain to your younger sibling how you cooked your lunch using just the sun and rain.
Think about solar panels! Just like plants capture sunlight to make food, humans learned to capture sunlight using solar panels to make electricity.
Find a green leaf near your house. Look closely at its surface. Can you spot the tiny veins that carry water? These are like the water pipes in your house!
Photosynthesis comes from two Greek words: 'photo' meaning light, and 'synthesis' meaning putting together. So it literally means putting things together using light!
Many students think plants get their food from the soil. The soil only provides water and minerals; the actual 'food' (sugar) is made inside the leaves!
Did you know there are plants that actually trap and eat insects? Or plants that steal food from other plants?
If a plant lives in very poor soil without enough nutrients, how do you think it survives?

content.title: The Venus Flytrap Trap
content.description: An animation showing a fly landing on the open leaves of a Venus Flytrap. The tiny hairs trigger, the leaves snap shut, and digestive juices slowly dissolve the fly.

content: Not all plants make their own food! Some, like the Pitcher plant or Venus flytrap, eat insects. These are called Insectivorous plants. Others, like the yellow, noodle-like Cuscuta (Amarbel), steal food from other plants. They are called Parasitic plants, and the plant they steal from is the Host.

question: Cuscuta (Amarbel) is an example of a:

content: Why do you think insectivorous plants need to eat insects if they are green and can do photosynthesis? Talk about it with a friend!
Insectivorous plants usually grow in soil that lacks nitrogen. They get their missing nitrogen by digesting the insects!
Parasites exist everywhere, not just in plants. Mosquitoes and ticks that bite humans are also parasites because they take nutrients from a host (you!).
Design your own imaginary insect-eating plant. Draw how it would look, what kind of trap it would use, and give it a cool name!
Have you ever seen fluffy white or green patches growing on old bread or leather shoes during the rainy season?
These patches aren't plants, and they don't have mouths. How do you think they 'eat' the bread?

content.title: Fungi Digestion
content.description: An animation zooming into a piece of bread showing microscopic fungi spreading thread-like roots (hyphae). They release juices onto the bread to melt it into a liquid, and then drink it up like a smoothie.

content: These organisms are called Fungi. Instead of eating solid food, they pour digestive juices on dead and decaying matter, turn it into a liquid, and absorb it. This unique way of eating is called Saprotrophic nutrition.

question: Organisms that feed on dead and decaying matter are called:

content: If fungi didn't exist to eat dead plants and animals, what would happen to our forests?
Fungi are nature's ultimate recyclers! By breaking down dead things, they return valuable nutrients back to the soil, which helps new plants grow. It's a perfect circle of life.
Sprinkle a few drops of water on a piece of bread and leave it in a warm, dark box for 2-3 days. Use a magnifying glass to observe the fungi (bread mould) that grows!
